title: Child asks 'why remember?': forget-by memory leases with recompute recipes
idea: A child asks why you'd keep every toy out forever. So each allocation carries a forget-by lease and a lineage recipe: the function and input handles that produced it. On expiry or memory pressure the OS drops the page and keeps only the recipe, and a later touch faults and recomputes it. This is Spark-RDD lineage moved down into virtual memory, aimed at caches, memo tables, decoded assets and derived indexes.
why: Derived data is often 30-50% of resident memory. Making it recompute-on-demand cuts resident DRAM 20-40% for cache-heavy services, paid for with spare CPU cycles.

title: Drop-shipping data: zero-inventory host memory for AI servers
idea: Like retailers that hold no stock and let suppliers ship direct, enforce a single-copy I/O path: storage DMAs straight into accelerator memory, page-cache and pinned bounce-buffer copies are eliminated, and the host keeps only metadata.
why: AI servers ship with 1-2 TB of host DRAM largely used as staging copies; could cut host DRAM 50-70% per node.

title: Minify KV vectors to 16-byte global product-quantized codes
idea: Minify each 128-dim FP16 key/value head vector (256 B) to a 16-byte product-quantization code against fleet-trained codebooks kept in on-chip SRAM. Attention scores are computed directly from lookup tables (asymmetric distance), never dequantizing.
why: 16x KV density on existing HBM and DRAM. The codebooks are shared by every session, so the overhead amortizes to zero.

title: Harvest LPDDR from recycled phones onto CXL cards
idea: Inverts 'consumer device memory dies with the device': e-waste recyclers desolder LPDDR4/4X packages from phones and laptops, reball and burn them in, and mount them on CXL cards with 28 nm controllers for slow capacity tiers.
why: Billions of retired devices hold 4-12 GB each, an exabyte-scale stranded bit supply that needs only existing OSAT lines and trailing-node controllers.

title: Bit-plane progressive memory with mantissa tails in flash
idea: Numeric arrays are stored transposed into bit-planes. DRAM holds the sign, exponent and top mantissa planes. The low-order planes live in CXL-attached flash and stream in only for operations flagged as precision-critical, such as optimizer updates. It is progressive JPEG for working memory, shifting from the bit scale to the tier scale.
why: BF16/FP32 tensors need 2-3x less DRAM when most kernels run on 6-8 effective bits. It also lowers the bandwidth spent per useful bit.

title: ECC check bits double as free dedup fingerprints
idea: TRIZ #6 Universality: the controller already computes SECDED/Chipkill check bytes for every 64 B line it writes; concatenating a page's check words yields a 512-byte signature that serves as a near-free dedup/similarity fingerprint, kept incrementally in a small on-chip table and byte-verified on a hit, so no CPU hashing or KSM-style scanning is needed.
why: Dedup is often disabled because hashing and scanning cost CPU and bandwidth; making it ~free recovers 5-25% of VM-host DRAM.

title: GPU texture units decode block-compressed weights at zero ALU cost
idea: Box: decompress × existing GPU texture-sampling hardware × 4×4 block × every fetch × BC4/BC5 (ASTC on mobile) endpoint-plus-index format. Weights are encoded as single- or dual-channel block-compressed textures by an encoder that minimizes matmul output error, and kernels fetch them through the texture path, which decompresses in fixed-function hardware.
why: ~4 bits per weight (4× smaller than FP16) with free random-access decode on silicon already shipped in every GPU, so no new chips and no fluorinated chemistry.

title: Regenerable pages: kernel drops pages tagged with rebuild functions
idea: IFR: memory holds only information that cannot be rebuilt. Closest: applications tag pages with a regenerator (re-decode image, re-decompress file, re-JIT, rebuild index) plus a cost hint; under pressure the kernel discards them like clean page cache and a userfaultfd handler rematerializes them on fault.
why: 15-30% of client and server RSS is derived data; reclaims it with no swap I/O and no new hardware.

title: Planar thin-film magnetic cores on glass revive core memory
idea: Core memory was byte-addressable, had unlimited endurance and needed no refresh; it lost only on size. Pattern micro-toroids of electroplated permalloy or ferrite with multi-turn copper windings on glass panels using panel-level packaging lithography (~10 um features), select them by coincident-current half-select and sense them inductively at ~100-300 ns.
why: A warm tier with no refresh and no wear, made in the US on panel-packaging tools; it can hold write-heavy warm data that flash tiers cannot, relieving silicon DRAM.

title: Rack-level spot market for gigabyte-seconds of pooled memory
idea: Treat DRAM as a perishable flow (GB-s), not a stock. Each rack's CXL memory pool runs a second-by-second auction in which jobs bid for leases that carry an eviction penalty, and the scheduler packs the bids so pooled DRAM runs at 85-90% utilization instead of the 50-60% of statically provisioned servers.
why: Recovers most of the 25-40% stranded memory in clouds, for ~15-25% fewer DRAM bits per unit of work; pool operators get a business model.

title: Rack memory commons: a domestic CXL switch pools all DRAM
idea: Po: servers own no memory. A CXL 3.x switch ASIC fabbed at GlobalFoundries Malta links 16-32 hosts to shared drawers of U.S.-made DRAM; hosts keep small local DIMMs and borrow the rest at ~250 ns, with the pool sized for the rack's aggregate peak, not the sum of per-host peaks.
why: Statistical multiplexing cuts provisioned DRAM 20-30% per rack, stretching scarce U.S.-made bits.

title: Content-addressed CXL switch acting as a rack memory CDN
idea: NICs hash cold 4 KB pages with BLAKE3 and publish them to a CXL switch that keeps a hash-to-physical map in on-switch SRAM. Identical pages from every server in the rack (container layers, libraries, zero pages, model shards, JIT code) collapse into one read-only copy in pooled memory, which every host maps.
why: Dedup on a single host gets 5-15%. Across hosts at rack scale on a homogeneous fleet it can reach 20-40% of the resident footprint.

title: Sub-second rack memory spot market over CXL
idea: Every 100 ms, the servers in a rack bid for 256 MB slices of pooled CXL memory. Each bid uses a price derived from that server's page-fault rate and SLO slack. An auctioneer in the switch reassigns slices, so stranded DRAM flows to whoever values it most at that instant.
why: Stranded or idle DRAM is 25-50% in clouds. Reallocating it every fraction of a second lets racks provision 20-30% less.

title: Single-mask polymer waveguide backplane for rack memory pooling
idea: One lithography mask patterns polymer optical waveguides directly into the rack backplane PCB. With existing co-packaged transceivers, they link 32 compute sleds to a shared memory sled. That makes rack-scale pooling cheap enough for each sled to ship with half its local DRAM.
why: Pooling recovers 25-50% stranded memory, so racks need 30-40% fewer DIMMs.

title: Pockels thin-film lithium niobate links make rack memory pooling viable
idea: Use thin-film LiNbO3 Pockels modulators (sub-pJ/bit, no carrier lifetime, ns latency) in CXL optical links so a rack-scale memory pool sits under 100 ns away. Servers keep a small local DRAM and borrow from the pool on demand, which removes per-server overprovisioning.
why: Stranded memory runs 25-35% in cloud fleets. Pooling recovers most of it, so each rack buys ~20% less DRAM.

title: Germanium photodetectors: optically pooled rack memory at 0.3 pJ/bit
idea: Ge-on-Si photodetectors and microring modulators in co-packaged optics connect every CPU in a rack to a shared memory pool at ~0.3 pJ/bit link energy over WDM, so servers ship with half their DRAM and borrow the rest from the pool on demand.
why: Pooling cuts stranded and overprovisioned DRAM 25-40% fleet-wide, and photonic links make a remote access cost ~10x less link energy than electrical CXL SerDes and retimers at rack distance (~3-5 pJ/bit) (capital, energy).

title: Laser-free rack memory pool over a passive copper backplane
idea: IFR: memory follows demand anywhere. Constraint: optical links need GaAs/InP lasers and InGaAs detectors (Ga, In), so stay electrical: a 1.5 m passive Cu twinax backplane and mature-node CXL switches with Al-Cu/Ti wiring pool DRAM across 16-32 hosts, sized to the P99 of the aggregate rather than each host's peak.
why: 20-30% less DRAM per rack with zero III-V parts.

title: Roll-to-roll polymer waveguide harness for rack memory pooling
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): multi-channel polymer optical waveguides are imprinted on meter-long flex film and laminated into a passive rack harness that links every server's CXL port to a shared memory appliance, replacing the costly active copper or fiber cabling that holds pooling back at scale.
why: Stranded and overprovisioned DRAM is 20-35% of fleet capacity; cheap pooling interconnect lets a rack share it, cutting installed DRAM ~15-25%.

title: Phase-change drift doubles as a built-in page age clock
idea: Give each page a Ge-rich GST cell that is reset on access. Structural relaxation makes its resistance drift upward as log(t), so reading the cell tells the controller the time since last use. A co-located reference cell drifts at the same 125 C temperature and normalizes the reading. Eviction to compressed or NVM tiers picks the oldest pages without timestamp SRAM.
why: Cheap, nonvolatile LRU age for every page enables aggressive tiering, with 30-50% less DRAM. Ge-rich GST retains data ~10 years at 150 C.

title: Memory-hard attacker's pebbling: compiler picks store versus recompute
idea: From attackers who evaluate memory-hard functions in tiny memory using pebbling strategies: a compiler pass solves a red-blue pebble game over any program's dataflow graph (databases, simulations, compilers, not only backprop) to choose per array whether to keep or recompute it, emitting a schedule that meets a declared memory cap.
why: Generalizes activation checkpointing to all software; typical 2-5x peak-memory cut for 10-30% extra compute.

title: Hardware page meshing merges half-empty pages
idea: Worsen: let fragmentation leave thousands of pages 10-30% full. Flip: the controller adds a sub-page remap table so two virtual pages whose live objects do not overlap share one physical frame, and a background engine finds mesh candidates from allocation bitmaps without moving objects.
why: Capacity: 15-40% less resident memory for fragmented heaps (Redis, browsers, Python) without a compacting GC.

title: Million slow TFT compressors on glass for cold pages
idea: Compressing cold pages is bound by throughput, not latency, so slow transistors suffice if there are enough of them. Tile a glass panel with ~1 million LTPS-TFT LZ/rANS engines at ~1-5 MHz each (aggregate >1e12 symbol operations/s), fed through optical I/O, which compress cold pages in the background and write them back to DRAM compacted.
why: Every server gets zswap-class 2-3x compression of cold memory without spending CPU cycles or silicon logic area.

title: Cache-resident streaming rings that skip DRAM entirely
idea: TRIZ #21 Skipping: NICs and SSDs inject data into an LLC-pinned ring (DDIO-style) whose credit-based flow control is matched to the consumer's processing rate, so streaming data is consumed and dropped before it is ever written back to DRAM.
why: Streaming analytics, packet processing and ETL hold large DRAM buffers only as staging; 5-10x smaller buffers and less write bandwidth.

title: Born-compressed tensors: math on codebook indices, never decompressed
idea: Po: data is born compressed and dies compressed. Weights and KV are stored as vector-quantized codebook indices, and the accelerator computes dot products from precomputed lookup tables of codeword-by-query partial products, never expanding values to FP16 in memory.
why: Keeps weights/KV at 2-3 bits per value in DRAM (5-8x smaller than FP16) and cuts data movement in proportion (fact 5).

title: Client-held KV cookies make chat servers stateless between turns
idea: Reverse who stores the conversation: after each turn the server compresses the session KV into a learned latent (~100-500 KB), encrypts and authenticates it, and returns it to the client like an HTTP cookie; the next request uploads it and the server expands it again.
why: Most chat KV sits idle while users read and type; dropping all idle-session state from server DRAM/HBM cuts KV memory 3-10x in consumer services.

title: Wire drawing: KV precision drawn down through successive dies with age
idea: Wire is pulled through a series of ever-smaller dies. Each KV token likewise passes through 'dies' as it ages and as its cumulative attention mass falls: FP16 to INT8 to INT4 to INT2, re-quantized in place by a background kernel. Each die's threshold is tuned so the perplexity loss stays below 0.1.
why: Long-context KV is dominated by old, rarely attended tokens, so average KV width drops from 16 bits to about 3, roughly a 5x capacity gain on the same HBM.

title: MicroLED-on-sapphire parallel links make pooled memory nearly free
idea: Pooling saves DRAM only if remote access costs nearly as much as local. GaN microLED and photodiode arrays grown on sapphire, coupled into glass imaging-fiber bundles, carry CXL traffic across a rack over hundreds of slow parallel lanes (~2 Gb/s each, no SerDes) at ~1 pJ/bit and low latency.
why: Makes rack-scale pooling viable even for latency-sensitive tiers, so operators provision ~20-30% less DRAM per server by reclaiming stranded memory.

title: Wafer stitching mask turning a DRAM wafer into shared pool
idea: One added top-metal stitching mask links reticle fields across the scribe lines, so an entire 300 mm DRAM wafer becomes one TB-scale memory fabric. Compute tiles bonded around it all read a single copy of the weights and shared KV prefixes, and defective fields are routed around.
why: Jumping from chip-scale to wafer-scale sharing collapses weight and prefix replication across 50-100 accelerators into one copy, cutting memory need 2-5x for large-model serving.

title: Sparse-HPC zero elision: pattern lines stored as metadata only
idea: From sparse-matrix HPC where most memory lines are zero: the controller keeps a per-line 2-bit pattern tag (zero, repeated byte, repeated word, real data) in ECC-adjacent metadata, so patterned lines consume no data storage and backing pages are reclaimed dynamically.
why: Sparse tensors, fresh allocations and padded buffers are often >90% patterned lines; eliding them cuts DRAM, and fab water, ~10x for those workloads.

title: Entropy-coded weights decoded inside registers, never materialized
idea: Inverts 'data must be decompressed before compute': weights stay Huffman/ANS-coded in DRAM and HBM and are decoded per tile into shared memory or registers inside the matmul kernel. The main target is BF16/FP8 exponent fields, which carry only ~2-3 bits of entropy.
why: Lossless 1.3-1.6x cut in weight footprint with bit-identical outputs, and it stacks with quantization.

title: Desert camel's stored fat: lossless entropy-coded weights decoded in shared memory
idea: A camel carries dense fat and converts it to water only when needed. BF16 weights live in HBM with the low-entropy exponent field Huffman-coded and the mantissa left raw. Each kernel decodes its tile into SM shared memory just before the matmul, so expanded weights never exist in DRAM.
why: The exponent carries about 2-3 bits of entropy out of 8, giving ~30% bit-exact compression with zero accuracy risk. Memory-bound decode also speeds up.

title: Lossless rANS-coded weights decoded inside the HBM base die
idea: IFR: weights are stored at their true information content. Closest: BF16/FP8 exponents (about 2.6 bits of entropy in 8) and top mantissa bits are rANS-coded per tensor, and line-rate decoders in the HBM/LPDDR logic die expand them so the host sees ordinary BF16.
why: ~30% lossless capacity and bandwidth gain on all weight memory with zero accuracy change; directly shrinks the HBM stacks needed per model.

title: Display-glass oxide-TFT warm tier priced by area, not wafer
idea: Cost per bit is area x cost per area, and processed display glass costs ~100-1000x less per cm^2 than a DRAM wafer. Build 1T1C arrays on Gen 8.5 glass on existing IGZO backplane lines, with large planar capacitors (no high-aspect-ratio etch) and ~1e-19 A/um leakage for minute-scale retention, packaged as a CXL warm tier at ~200 ns-1 us.
why: Even with a cell 100x larger than silicon DRAM, cost per bit can be ~5-10x lower. Warm pages move there, so silicon DRAM shrinks to the hot set (30-50% less), using idle LCD capacity.

title: Minify weights to seeds: on-chip PRNG regenerates weight blocks
idea: Minify stored weights to an LFSR seed plus a few coefficients per block. On-chip PRNG units regenerate a pseudo-random basis and combine it into the weights at matmul time, after a seed search at compression time.
why: ~10x weight compression (16 bits down to ~1.5 effective bits) by converting memory into cheap on-die logic and FLOPs.

title: Weights stored as PRNG seeds plus a few coefficients
idea: Inverts 'weights are stored numbers': each block of weights is approximated as a combination of a few pseudo-random basis vectors that an on-chip LFSR generates from a stored seed, so DRAM holds seeds and 4-bit coefficients instead of weights.
why: Effective 2-3 bits per weight, trading cheap compute for memory; the generator costs a few gates per lane.

title: Seed-generated weights: LFSR seeds plus coefficients replace stored matrices
idea: Box: procedural generation × accelerator load path × 8×8 weight block × decode at GEMM time × 16-bit LFSR seed + 4 coefficients. Each block is a fitted combination of pseudo-random basis vectors regenerated by an on-chip LFSR, so memory holds ~3–4 bits per weight with no codebook to fetch.
why: 4–5× less weight memory than BF16 and fewer bytes moved per FLOP; logic is cheap while DRAM bits are scarce.

title: Potassium-40 seeds: weights stored as PRNG seeds plus coefficients
idea: K-40's natural decay is randomness for free; each 8x8 weight block is stored as a 16-bit LFSR seed plus four 4-bit coefficients that mix the pseudo-random basis vectors the seed generates, and the accelerator regenerates the basis on the fly with a few gates per lane.
why: About 3-4 bits per weight with no codebook memory; LLM weight DRAM falls 4-5x vs bf16, and more for cold experts (density, cost/bit).

title: Connection Machine, fixed: bit-serial compute inside cache SRAM arrays
idea: Thinking Machines' CM-1 used 65,536 bit-serial processors with private memory and died on cost and programmability. Do bit-serial compute inside existing SRAM subarrays by activating two wordlines and sensing bitline AND/NOR on transposed data, so each bitline is a processor and activations are processed where they sit.
why: Activations never leave SRAM, so DRAM staging buffers between layers disappear for small and mid-size models.

title: HP The Machine, minus memristor: rack single-copy read-only data
idea: HP's The Machine died because its memristor never shipped, orphaning a sound idea: fabric-attached memory shared by many nodes. Use CXL 3 shared memory with commodity DRAM to hold exactly one rack-wide copy of read-only data (model weights, reference genomes, dictionaries, container layers) mapped read-only into every host.
why: Eliminates N per-host copies; for a 16-host rack serving the same models, weight DRAM drops ~10x.

title: Synaptic tag-and-capture promotes only reinforced KV entries
idea: New KV entries are written provisionally at 2-4 bit into a small scratch ring carrying a decaying 'tag'; only entries that receive above-threshold attention mass while tagged 'capture' promotion to full-precision storage, mirroring synaptic tagging and capture in long-term potentiation. Untagged entries expire or remain as 2-bit sketches.
why: KV capacity: most tokens never receive meaningful attention; 3-6x KV footprint reduction with bounded accuracy loss.

title: Mainframe-style page-only DRAM die strips column periphery
idea: Combine IBM's expanded-storage concept (page-addressable-only memory) with a DRAM die redesign: a die accessed only in 4 KB blocks drops fine column decoders, most data-path muxing and per-bank DLL logic, giving much of the ~49% periphery area back to cells on a DUV node; it serves as the tier below byte-addressable DRAM.
why: ~1.4-1.7x bits per mm2 on non-EUV nodes (fact 7) at the cost of block access; main DRAM shrinks because cold pages live here.

title: Error-bounded scientific compression built into the memory controller
idea: Combine ZFP/SZ-style transform coding with the memory controller: pages tagged approximate-OK (simulation fields, activations, gradients) are stored at fixed rates of 8-16 bits per float with guaranteed absolute error bounds, using fixed-rate blocks so random access stays O(1).
why: 2-4x capacity for floating-point working sets that tolerate bounded error.

title: TSV-stacked read-optimized NAND beside the accelerator for weights
idea: Combine HBM-style TSV stacking and wide I/O on a mature-node base die with NAND dies tuned for massive read parallelism, dedicated to read-only inference weights; the accelerator's HBM keeps only KV cache and activations.
why: Weights are read-only so NAND endurance is irrelevant; 8-16x capacity per stack versus HBM DRAM, with no EUV layer in either the NAND or the base die.

title: Internal GB-second market where memory-hungry jobs must bid
idea: Inverts 'memory is free once the server is bought': the cluster scheduler prices resident memory per GB-second at a spot price set by scarcity. Elastic consumers (caches, JVM heaps, prefetch buffers) register demand curves and shrink automatically when the price rises.
why: Fleets strand 25-40% of DRAM in over-requested allocations; price signals reclaim much of it with no new hardware.

title: Cold-chain use-by dates: TTL-typed memory in refresh-free banks
idea: Borrowed from perishable-food logistics where every pallet carries a use-by date: allocations carry a time-to-live (malloc_ttl, compiler-known tensor lifetimes), and the controller places sub-retention lifetimes in banks with refresh permanently disabled, built with ~5x smaller capacitors that only need ~10 ms retention; long-lived data goes to SRAM or non-volatile tiers.
why: Zero refresh power for the ephemeral majority (activations, request heaps, packet buffers); small-capacitor ephemeral cells sidestep the 60-75:1 charge wall for denser, cheaper bits.

title: Refresh cycles fused with page fingerprinting for in-DRAM dedup
idea: Combine the mandatory refresh operation with content hashing: a tiny CRC/hash unit at each subarray's sense amplifiers folds every row into a 32-bit signature as it is refreshed and writes it to a reserved signature row. The controller reads the signature table every 64 ms, verifies candidate matches and merges duplicate pages by remapping, replacing CPU-driven KSM scanning.
why: Dedup recovers 10-40% of capacity on VM/container hosts but today costs CPU and bandwidth to scan; piggybacking on refresh (fact 3) makes always-on dedup nearly free, so fewer DRAM bits per host.

title: Bus timetable: compiled exact page-in schedule for model inference
idea: Inference access order is as fixed as a bus timetable: the compiler emits a cycle-accurate schedule of which weight/KV pages must arrive when, and a DMA engine streams them from flash or CXL into a DRAM ring sized for ~2 layers plus slack, with no demand paging at all.
why: Batch/offline inference needs only the in-flight window resident; DRAM per model drops 10-50x when flash bandwidth covers per-layer compute time.

title: Park idle chat sessions as token IDs, re-prefill in FLOP valleys
idea: Box: recompute × inference runtime × whole-session KV × idle >30 s × backing = 2-byte token IDs. Idle sessions drop their KV cache (~100–300 KB per token for large models) and keep only token IDs; when the user returns, a scheduler re-prefills the context in bursts on compute left idle between decode steps.
why: Trades abundant FLOPs for scarce bytes at ~10^5:1 compression of parked state; cuts resident KV in multi-tenant chat serving 3–10× because most sessions are idle most of the time.

title: Eliminate redundant buffer copies with OS move-semantics page ownership
idea: The OS gains a linear-ownership primitive: a buffer moves from NIC to kernel to app to serializer by page remapping with the old mapping revoked, so a request path holds one copy of data instead of 3-4.
why: Network-heavy services hold 2-4 copies of each payload; collapsing them cuts buffer DRAM 50-75%.

title: Free-before-allocate runtimes shrink garbage-collected heap headroom
idea: Reverse GC's allocate-then-find-garbage order: compiler region inference and escape analysis free most objects deterministically at scope exit, and a forwarding table in the memory controller lets the remaining collector compact concurrently, so heaps run at ~1.2x live data instead of 2-3x.
why: Java, Go and .NET fleets hold a large share of datacenter DRAM; cutting heap headroom 30-50% translates directly into fewer DIMMs.

title: Shannon-metered inline rANS coding in the memory controller
idea: First principles: a byte of typical server heap carries only ~2-4 bits of Shannon entropy, so storing 8 bits is pure waste. Put a table-driven rANS (asymmetric numeral system) codec in the memory controller, with frequency tables per page class learned online by a sampling engine; 4 KB pages live in variable-size 512 B sub-blocks tracked by a small translation table, and hot lines are cached decompressed.
why: Capacity per installed bit: 1.8-2.5x effective DRAM on heaps and caches, measured against the entropy bound, for ~5-10 ns of decode on misses; cuts the DRAM bought per server directly.

title: Entropy-sized pointers: hardware 32-bit region-relative pointer storage
idea: A 64-bit pointer inside a heap carries only log2(reachable objects), about 28-34 bits of information. The allocator sets a per-page pointer-map bit; the memory controller stores tagged words as 32-bit offsets from a per-1 GB region base held in page metadata and re-expands them on load.
why: Pointer-dense workloads (graphs, JVM/Go heaps, key-value stores, B-trees) are 30-50% pointers; halving them saves 15-25% of DRAM at ~1 cycle of expand latency.

title: Nanoimprinted via-ROM weight tape laminated onto a readout die
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): frozen model weights are encoded as present or absent conductive vias in a roll-to-roll nanoimprinted passive crossbar (~200 nm pitch, ~25 Tb/m2) with printed Schottky contacts to block sneak paths, laminated face-to-face onto a small silicon sense-amp die that reads whole rows in parallel. Nothing active is printed; only the bit pattern is.
why: Weights are the largest frozen block in inference DRAM; moving them into printed ROM costing dollars per m2 could cut accelerator DRAM per model 2-5x with no EUV and no DRAM fab capacity.

title: Spin-orbit domain-wall racetrack serves the append-only KV cache
idea: The KV cache is written only at its tail and read in full order every decode step, which is exactly a racetrack's access pattern. SOT current pulses shift magnetic domain walls along nanowires, appending each new token at the write head and streaming all tokens past a read head once per step. No random-access decoders or row activations are needed.
why: At ~1-2F^2 per bit with no refresh, the KV tier costs 3-5x less per bit than DRAM (facts 1, 3, 8).

title: Learned models plus Elias–Fano offsets replace pointer-heavy indexes
idea: Box: representation shrink × database engine × index × build time × piecewise-linear model + succinct leaf offsets. B-tree inner nodes and hash-index pointers become small learned position models with Elias–Fano coded offsets queried by rank/select.
why: Indexes take 20–50% of in-memory database DRAM; learned plus succinct encodings shrink them 10–100×.

title: Wine-cellar racking: match data lifetime to each row's retention
idea: Borrowed from cellars that put long-aging vintages in the coolest, most stable racks: a boot-time and online profiler bins every row by measured retention (most rows hold 1-10 s, only a tail is near 64 ms), and the OS places each page by its predicted rewrite interval into a row that outlasts it; pages with uncertain lifetimes go to a non-volatile shelf.
why: Removes refresh by exploiting the retention distribution instead of designing for the 13 fA tail; recovers 16-33% of idle power and keeps weak-retention dies in service, raising usable supply.

title: Eliminate duplicate lines with content-addressed main memory in CXL expanders
idea: A CXL memory expander stores 64B lines by hash in a deduplicated store with reference counts; host physical addresses map to hash entries, so identical lines across VMs and containers are stored once.
why: VM and container fleets have 20-50% duplicate content: 1.25-2x capacity per installed bit.

title: Antifuse weight ROM banks rotate through over-the-air model updates
idea: Freeze automotive perception weights into oxide-breakdown antifuse arrays with in-array MAC. Ship 8 banks and burn one per model release, so each OTA update takes a fresh bank. A broken-down oxide filament is permanent at 125 C.
why: ECUs need no DRAM for weights. Antifuse is 28 nm logic-compatible, U.S.-manufacturable and needs no EUV (fact 4).

title: Warehouse cross-docking: I/O buffers skip DRAM, land in cache
idea: Borrowed from cross-dock logistics where pallets go straight from inbound to outbound trucks: NIC and NVMe DMA writes are steered into reserved LLC/accelerator-SRAM 'dock doors' with a scheduled consumer appointment, and the consumer's completion frees the door; only overflow spills to DRAM. A hardware yard scheduler enforces the appointment windows.
why: Network/storage staging buffers take GBs per server and double DRAM traffic; removing the staging copy cuts buffer DRAM 80-90% and saves ~2 DRAM passes per byte.

title: Blurry numbers: error-bounded compression of live simulation state
idea: Po: numbers are blurry on purpose. DOE-lab error-bounded lossy compressors (SZ/ZFP class) run inline in the memory path of U.S.-built supercomputer nodes, keeping field data compressed under a user-set pointwise error bound and decompressing per tile on access.
why: Scientific floating-point fields compress 5-20x within physics-acceptable error, so domestic HPC fits larger problems in the same DRAM.

title: Pacemaker compressive sensing: store random projections, not samples
idea: From microwatt implants that store ECG as sparse projections: sensor and telemetry streams are written to memory as compressive-sensing measurements (random +/-1 projections computed in the NIC), and a sparse-recovery engine reconstructs a window only when it is actually queried.
why: Sparse signals (vibration, network flows, sensor feeds) need 4-10x fewer measurements than samples and most stored windows are never read, so buffering DRAM drops 4-10x.

title: Load-and-kill instruction frees memory at a value's last use
idea: IFR: memory frees itself the instant data is dead. Closest: a compiler-emitted load-and-kill instruction marks a line or page dead after its final read; the cache drops it without writeback and the OS reclaims fully dead frames immediately.
why: Cuts temporary-buffer footprint 10-20% in streaming and ML pipelines and removes useless writeback bandwidth.

title: Air-freight belly cargo: harvest stranded memory inside peripherals
idea: Borrowed from airlines selling spare cargo space under passenger cabins: idle DRAM in SmartNICs, DPUs, SSD controllers, BMCs and HBM on under-used inference cards is exported as a unified low-priority tier over PCIe/CXL, with a broker that preempts it when the device needs it back.
why: Peripheral DRAM can be 10-30% of a server's total and is mostly idle; harvesting it cuts host DIMM purchases by a similar fraction.

title: Firmware-style unikernels erase per-VM operating system footprint
idea: From single-purpose embedded firmware: cloud services are linked with only the library-OS components they use into unikernels on a thin hypervisor, removing the general-purpose kernel, init system and page cache from every VM.
why: A general guest OS idles at 200-500 MB versus 5-20 MB for a unikernel; small-service fleets cut per-instance DRAM 10x+ and fab water accordingly.

title: Low-Vt implant mask for bank-edge LUT dequantizers
idea: One added low-Vt implant mask speeds up a strip of periphery transistors next to each bank enough to run a 16-entry LUT dequantizer at internal row speed. Weights and KV are stored at 3-4 bits and expanded to BF16 at the bank edge, so neither capacity nor external bandwidth pays for full precision.
why: 4-5x less DRAM capacity for quantized weights and KV with no host-side dequantization cost. Unmodified DRAM periphery transistors are too slow to do this.

title: Zinc sacrificial anode: hardware-droppable pages for regenerable data
idea: Zinc corrodes first to protect steel; software tags regenerable data (decompressed copies, JIT code, memo tables, page-cache clones) as sacrificial in the page table, and under pressure the memory controller zeroes and reassigns those frames in microseconds without OS swapping, raising a fault so the data is rebuilt if touched again.
why: Servers can run with 20-30% less DRAM headroom because the spare capacity lives inside regenerable caches that are reclaimed instantly (cost/bit, capital).

title: Adiabatic reversible logic makes recomputing activations cheaper than storing
idea: Run on-device adaptation with reversible network layers (RevNet-style) on charge-recovery adiabatic logic. Activations are recomputed backward from outputs at ~10x less switching energy, so they are never stored. Adiabatic switching also cuts self-heating, keeping junctions inside budget at 125 C ambient.
why: On-device fine-tuning memory falls 5-10x because activations are not stored.

title: Half-size pointers: base-relative 32-bit addressing in the ISA
idea: Po: addresses cost nothing. An ISA extension adds region-base registers and load/store forms taking 32-bit (or 24-bit) offsets with hardware base addition, so C/C++/Rust programs and runtimes use compressed pointers everywhere, not only in JVM compressed oops.
why: Pointer-heavy data (graphs, trees, object heaps) is 30-50% pointers; halving them cuts footprint 15-25% and raises cache density.

title: Drum optimum-programming assembler that fills every opened DRAM row
idea: Port the IBM 650 SOAP idea (place each word where the drum will be when it is needed) to DRAM rows: a placement pass lays out embedding rows, sparse KV blocks and gather targets so bytes consumed together by one kernel share one 1-2 KB row, keeping re-transposed copies per consumer when reuse justifies it. The memory controller then replays a compile-time row schedule instead of reacting to random requests.
why: Fact 8 (128x overfetch, ~5.9 pJ per useful bit): raising useful bytes per activation from ~1/128 to ~1/4 cuts random-access energy 10-30x and frees channel bandwidth, so fewer DRAM devices meet the same throughput.

title: Physarum tube-reinforcement solver places pages across pooled CXL memory
idea: Each host-to-memory-node path is modeled as a slime-mould tube whose conductance grows with page traffic and decays otherwise; pages migrate along thickening tubes, so the pool converges on a minimal network where a shared page lives once, near its heaviest consumers, instead of being replicated per host.
why: Stranded and replicated DRAM in racks: 20-35% less total DRAM at near-local latency.

title: Permute weight channels so neighbors compress, then delta-code
idea: Rearrange the order of rows and channels inside each weight matrix (with the matching permutation folded into the next layer) so similar channels sit side by side, then store each channel as a low-bit delta from its predecessor.
why: Adds ~1.3-2x near-lossless compression on top of quantization for weights held in existing DRAM; the permutation is free at runtime and needs no new hardware.

title: Overlay-tree linker streams MoE experts into fixed HBM slots
idea: Revive 1960s overlay trees (IBM 7090/1401 linkers): the model compiler builds a static overlay tree with a resident root (attention, router, shared experts) and N fixed overlay slots, and experts load from LPDDR/NVMe into those slots one layer ahead using a cheap speculative router run on layer L's hidden state. Overlay loads are fixed DMA scripts generated at compile time, not demand paging.
why: Capacity: MoE models leave 90%+ of weights idle per token; holding only root plus slots cuts HBM footprint 3-6x for small-batch serving with <10% latency hit when routing prediction is >90% accurate.

title: Williams tube rebuilt with Spindt emitters over unpatterned charge target
idea: Revive the Williams/BEAMOS tube in flat form: a university-fabricated Spindt field-emitter array gated by row/column lines addresses spots on an unpatterned SiO2-on-Si charge-storage target a few microns away in vacuum. Bits are written by secondary-emission charging and read as target current, so the storage plane needs no cell lithography and no per-bit transistor.
why: A bulk capacity tier with near-zero cell processing (no EUV, no capacitor, no tungsten) behind a much smaller DRAM cache; addressing lives entirely in a reusable emitter array.

title: Speech-codec linear prediction stores KV cache as residuals
idea: Borrowed from LPC/CELP voice codecs: a tiny per-head linear predictor estimates layer L's keys/values from layer L-1 and the previous token, and only the 1-2 bit quantized prediction residual is stored; predictor coefficients are an offline-fitted codebook. The attention kernel recomputes prediction plus residual on read.
why: KV cache dominates inference DRAM; exploiting cross-layer/cross-token redundancy like speech's formant structure could give 4-8x over 16-bit KV, beyond plain quantization.

title: One latent per token regenerates every layer's K/V on demand
idea: Inverts 'each layer stores its own KV cache': DRAM holds a single low-rank latent per token (e.g., 256 dims), and each layer's tensor cores up-project it to K and V just in time inside the attention kernel, spending cheap FLOPs to save scarce bytes. A short distillation pass retrofits existing models so the shared cross-layer latent is trained jointly.
why: KV-cache bytes drop 10-40x vs per-layer FP16 KV, beyond per-layer latent attention, so long-context serving fits in a fraction of the HBM/DRAM.

title: Sky-survey neural fields: datasets stored as tiny networks
idea: From astronomy surveys drowning in petabytes of images: large read-mostly arrays (images, volumes, simulation snapshots, maps) are fitted into compact hash-grid neural fields and queried by evaluating the network at coordinates on the accelerator, with a residual store only where error exceeds the bound.
why: Neural fields reach 10-100x compression on smooth data, so resident DRAM per dataset falls 10x+ and fab water with it.

title: Follow-the-night DRAM provisioning across continents
idea: The global fleet is treated as one memory pool over 24 hours. Deferrable memory-heavy jobs (embedding rebuilds, batch inference, index builds, ETL) are routed to whichever region is in its diurnal trough. Each region's DRAM is then sized for the flattened global curve, not for its local evening peak.
why: Fleets provision DRAM for peak, and diurnal peak-to-trough is 1.5-2x. This means 15-30% fewer DIMMs fleetwide with zero new silicon.

title: Reversible layers fused with backprop eliminate activation storage
idea: Combine reversible (bijective) residual blocks with training: activations are reconstructed exactly from layer outputs during the backward pass instead of being stored, using fixed-point coupling functions so reconstruction never drifts.
why: Activation memory, often the largest training footprint, becomes constant in depth, cutting training DRAM/HBM 3-10x on any hardware including mature-node accelerators.

title: Reversible layers reconstruct activations instead of storing them
idea: Box: invertibility × model architecture × layer activations × backward pass × additive coupling blocks. Training uses invertible residual blocks whose inputs are recomputed exactly from outputs during backpropagation, so per-layer activations are never kept.
why: Activation memory becomes constant in depth, 5–10× less training memory; mathematics only, no fluorinated inputs.

title: Freeze-dried heap: dehydrate cold objects, rehydrate on touch
idea: Borrowed from freeze-drying food: the garbage collector moves objects untouched for N cycles into a 'dehydrated' arena where pointers become 24-bit arena-relative varints, headers are dropped and fields are entropy-coded; a load barrier rehydrates an object into the live heap on first access.
why: Managed-language heaps (Java, Python, JS) are 50-70% cold and pointer-bloated; 2-4x footprint reduction on the cold majority.

title: 28 nm SRAM-chain pipeline with codebook weights replaces DRAM
idea: Combine weight-stationary pipeline parallelism across many 28 nm SRAM-rich chips (~300 MB each) with 2-3-bit vector-quantized codebook weights decoded at the MAC array, so a whole model lives in mature-node SRAM spread along a board-level chain.
why: Eliminates DRAM for inference with all-DUV, U.S.-fabbable silicon, trading more die area for zero EUV, zero DRAM and very high bandwidth.

title: Doppelganger cache, fixed: approximate dedup of near-identical KV blocks
idea: The Doppelganger approximate cache (2015) mapped similar-valued blocks to one copy but died because general programs need exact data. LLM KV caches tolerate it: LSH-hash each 16-token KV block and map blocks within cosine >0.995 across requests and layers to one physical block plus a small residual.
why: Shared-context and templated workloads see 1.5-3x KV footprint reduction, and KV dominates inference DRAM/HBM.

title: Monk with one bowl: eBPF census finds duplicate buffer copies
idea: A monk owns one bowl, not five. An eBPF plus page-hash census tool samples contents across the page cache, socket buffers, user heaps and GPU staging buffers and flags identical data held in two or more places (the NIC-kernel-user-serialize-GPU chain). The team then ships upstream zero-copy patches (io_uring registered buffers, splice, mmap'd page cache) for the top offenders.
why: Data-path services hold 2-5 copies of in-flight data. A small team can free 10-25% of DRAM on storage, proxy and ingest nodes.

title: Bucket brigade: oxide-TFT charge-transfer FIFO for pipelined activations
idea: Firefighters pass buckets down a line: build a back-end IGZO charge-transfer shift-register (CCD-like) memory that supports only FIFO access, eliminating row decoders and most sense amps, and use it for pipeline-parallel activation queues and streamed weights, which are naturally sequential.
why: Periphery is ~49% of the DRAM die (fact 7); a decoder-less FIFO memory reaches ~2x bit density and replaces DRAM for sequential buffers, all at <=400 C.

title: Swap scrapped retention-fail dies for an error-tolerant DRAM grade
idea: Substitute 'scrap' with 'approximate grade'. Dies that fail retention or margin screens are packaged as standard DDR5/LPDDR5 parts rated for a measured bit-error rate, and the OS and ML frameworks place only error-tolerant data on them (activations, media buffers, refetchable caches). DDR/HBM interfaces are unchanged.
why: Adds sellable bits with no new wafers by recovering several percent of test fallout, and loosens the leakage-tail screen (fact 3).

title: AI-grade binning: sell failing DRAM dies to fault-tolerant workloads
idea: Inverts 'every die must pass full spec': dies from existing lines that fail retention screens or have clustered bad rows get a per-die bad-row map in a 40 nm controller's fuse table. They are sold as 'AI-grade' modules for weights and KV, where row remapping plus tensor-level checksums hide the defects.
why: Recovers several % of wafer output that is now scrapped or downbinned, so existing fabs yield more usable bits with no new capacity.

title: Stock reduction: simmer near-duplicate tokens into weighted KV entries
idea: As a chef reduces stock to concentrate flavour, a background pass merges runs of KV entries whose keys are near-duplicates into one centroid entry carrying a count that adds log(count) to its attention logit, preserving attention mass.
why: Long contexts are full of repetitive tokens; 2-5x fewer stored KV entries for documents and code with attention mass conserved on merged clusters.

title: Sealed-submarine contract: applications negotiate memory like video bitrate
idea: From submarines that must keep running as hardware fails during months sealed: an OS API (memory.qos) lets apps register quality-versus-footprint ladders (cache size, model precision, index granularity), and the kernel steps each app down or up the ladder under pressure instead of swapping or OOM-killing.
why: Lets fleets provision for typical rather than peak memory: 20-40% fewer DIMMs with graceful quality loss.

title: Weight radio: one DRAM read broadcast to 32 accelerators
idea: Inverts 'every accelerator needs its own copy of the weights': many small inference cards march in lockstep through the same layer while one shared DDR4 pool streams each weight tile once over a multicast fabric built from existing 28 nm FPGAs and SerDes. Each card applies the tile to its own batch.
why: Weight DRAM drops N-fold (e.g., 32x) across a pod, using trailing-node accelerators and legacy DRAM.

title: MP3 bit reservoir: fixed compressed slots with borrowed bits
idea: MP3 frames borrow unused bits from a shared reservoir to hold a constant bitrate; likewise every compressed page gets a fixed 2 KB slot (address = index x 2 KB, no translation table) and pages that overflow borrow 256 B chunks from a per-region reservoir located via a tiny overflow bitmap.
why: Variable-size memory compression needs translation tables and fragmentation handling that add latency; fixed slots plus a reservoir keep O(1) addressing while capturing ~1.8-2x capacity.

title: Blast chiller: compress lines at LLC eviction straight into NV log
idea: Like blast chillers freezing food before ice crystals form, a 'chiller' engine at the last-level cache compresses evicted lines predicted cold and appends them directly to a persistent NAND/MRAM log on CXL, bypassing DRAM; reads of chilled lines return through a small decompress buffer.
why: Cold data never occupies DRAM even briefly and is durable on arrival; claims a 2-3x smaller DRAM tier with persistence included.

title: Fly mushroom-body hashing finds near-duplicate pages for delta storage
idea: Fruit flies tag odors via random sparse expansion then winner-take-all; the controller applies the same FlyHash to sampled page contents to bucket near-duplicates, storing each as a delta against a bucket representative (checkpoints, VM snapshots, model replicas with slight drift).
why: Capacity: catches near-duplicates that exact-hash dedup misses, a further 1.3-2x.

title: Copper-style overlay sequencer streaming model layers from parallel flash
idea: TRIZ #10 Prior action: a compiler precomputes a full 1980s-style overlay schedule of which weight tiles are needed when, and a 180 nm microcoded DMA sequencer (like the Amiga Copper) executes it, streaming tiles from 16-32 parallel NAND channels into a small DRAM ring one or two layers ahead of compute.
why: Deterministic batch inference needs only ~2 layers resident; 5-20x less weight DRAM, using only old-node control logic.

title: Memory-footprint budgets written into federal software procurement
idea: Combine the software bill of materials (SBOM) requirement with a measured memory-footprint disclosure: federally procured software must report peak and steady-state RSS on standardized workloads, and contracts score bids on GB per transaction.
why: Shifts demand: a 20-30% cut in software bloat across government and contractors frees DRAM supply without fabs, and the disclosure norm spreads to industry.

title: Iron hemoglobin carrier: data stays compressed until it reaches registers
idea: Hemoglobin carries O2 bound and releases it only at the tissue; lines stay base-delta/FPC compressed in DRAM, on the bus and in L2/LLC, and a decompressor in the core's load pipeline expands them only into registers, with ALU support for compares and adds directly on base-delta values.
why: Capacity and bandwidth gains arrive together (1.5-2x effective DRAM) without decompressed duplicates anywhere in the hierarchy (cost/bit, energy).

title: Fluoropolymer nonstick tensors: activations flow chiplet-to-chiplet, never landing in DRAM
idea: PTFE is the fluorine-carbon coating nothing sticks to; the compiler maps inference layers as a spatial pipeline across chiplets so activations stream SRAM-to-SRAM over 0.1-0.3 pJ/bit die-to-die links with credit flow control, and DRAM never stores activations or partial sums.
why: Each DRAM write plus read of an activation costs ~20-30 pJ/bit versus ~0.3 pJ/bit on package, a 50-100x saving for that traffic, and activation buffer DRAM disappears (energy, density).
